items.title: 68427_Harry Edison oral history interview
items.q: I met him with then, named Harold Arnold, he was a tenor player. So he and I were good friends.

ctx.x: Yeah, the Reno Club. They all went back to join Basie. And about that time, Lucky Millinder sent a telegram to some trumpet player there in St. Louis he wanted to come but he sent tickets to a friend of mine who was playing with the St. Louis Crackerjacks. I met him with then, named Harold Arnold, he was a tenor player. So he and I were good friends. So he said, 'Well, I got a ticket here so I have to get the trumpet player Lucky sent for.' So he said, 'Why don't you take the ticket and let's both go to New York.
So I said, "Well, he didn't send for me, he sent for somebody else." So he said, "What difference does it make," you know. So, okay, we got on the train and went to New York.

items.title: Harry Edison — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: And I knew Harold Arnold who enticed me to go to New York on this fake ticket under somebody else’s name.

ctx.x: Was he soloing like he eventually did with Duke?

Oh yeah, he was soloing then, he was soloing while the band was playing. But he soloed in a way that he still was swinging. And he was just with Jeter-Pillars for a short time. Then Ellington came through there and snatched him away. At that time the big band used to come through St. Louis all the time, they were taking everybody. Later on, they got Harold Baker, Shorty Baker. He went with Don Redman first, then he went with Ellington. That’s the way I got to New York, really. It was really funny how I got to New…
But you didn’t try and go under the name of Harold Baker.
